title: Contrastive training and InfoNCE
summary: InfoNCE is cross entropy over the passages in your batch, temperature decides which negatives your gradient actually pays attention to, and in-batch negatives give quadratic training signal for linear compute. The denominator is what fixes the anisotropy from Day 10.
html:
Day 10 ended with a broken instrument. A raw transformer's embeddings sit in a narrow cone, every pair scores around 0.8, and an ordering built on that is close to noise. Pooling cannot fix it. Today is what does.

Say what you want, directly

You want similar texts close and dissimilar texts far apart. Nothing in language modelling optimises for that. Predicting the next token does not require a well-spread geometry, so you do not get one.

So train for it. Collect examples of the thing you want, triples of a query, a passage that answers it, and passages that do not:

query:     "how do bees make honey?"
positive:  "workers fan the open cells until water content falls below 18 percent..."
negatives: ["the queen lays up to 2000 eggs per day...",
            "drones cannot sting or forage...",
            "TCP uses a three way handshake..."]

Then push the query toward the positive and away from the negatives. That is contrastive learning in one sentence. Everything else is how you turn it into a loss with a usable gradient.

InfoNCE, which is just softmax classification

L = -log[  exp( sim(q, p+) / T )  /  SUM_i exp( sim(q, p_i) / T )  ]

That looks like a mouthful and it is one idea you already know. Read the bracket: it is a softmax over candidates, and the loss is the negative log probability of the right one. This is cross entropy for a classification problem where the classes are the passages in front of you.

The task is: given this query and B candidate passages, pick the one that answers it. Standard classification, except the class set changes every batch and the "classifier" is the geometry of the embedding space itself. Get it right and the loss is near zero. Rank a negative above the positive and the loss is large. Gradients flow into the encoder and move both the query and the passages.

Temperature is a gradient allocation knob

T divides every similarity before the softmax. It is not a nuisance parameter. It decides which negatives your gradient pays attention to.

Take one query with a positive at cosine 0.80 and negatives at 0.75, 0.70, 0.40 and 0.10:

T = 1.00    P(positive) = 0.249   P(hardest neg) = 0.236   loss = 1.392
T = 0.20    P(positive) = 0.392   P(hardest neg) = 0.305   loss = 0.936
T = 0.05    P(positive) = 0.665   P(hardest neg) = 0.245   loss = 0.408
T = 0.01    P(positive) = 0.993   P(hardest neg) = 0.007   loss = 0.007

At T = 1 the model barely distinguishes the positive from the hardest negative, a ratio of 1.05, so the gradient is smeared across everything including the obviously irrelevant TCP passage. At T = 0.01 the positive already takes 99.3 percent of the mass, the loss is 0.007, and there is almost no gradient left. The model has stopped learning from this example even though a negative sits 0.05 away.

Low temperature concentrates the gradient on whichever negatives are closest to the positive. That is usually what you want, because those are the ones actually hurting retrieval. Push it too low and training destabilises, because a single mislabelled negative now dominates the update. Published models cluster around 0.01 to 0.1, and 0.05 is a common default. It is genuinely a tuned hyperparameter, not a derived constant.

In-batch negatives, and why batch size dominates

Here is the trick that makes this practical, and it has a shape you will like.

Take a batch of B query-positive pairs. Encode all of them: 2B forward passes. Now compute the full B by B similarity matrix. For query i, the diagonal entry is its positive and every other column is a negative you got for free, because those passages belong to other queries in the batch and almost certainly do not answer this one.

batch      8:      16 forward passes ->              64 scores,      7 negatives/query
batch     64:     128 forward passes ->           4,096 scores,     63 negatives/query
batch   1024:   2,048 forward passes ->       1,048,576 scores,  1,023 negatives/query
batch  32768:  65,536 forward passes -> 1,073,741,824 scores, 32,767 negatives/query

Compute grows linearly in B. Training signal grows quadratically. Double the batch and you pay twice for four times the pairs. That is why embedding papers report batch sizes in the tens of thousands while a classifier is happy at 32, and why batch size is reported like a headline number in this literature rather than buried in an appendix.

You cannot get there naively, because B sequences of activations do not fit in memory. The standard answer is GradCache: run the forward passes in chunks without gradients, cache the embeddings, compute the loss over the full matrix, then recompute gradients chunk by chunk. You trade compute for memory to buy a bigger effective batch. It is the same bargain as gradient checkpointing, aimed at a different bottleneck.

Why this fixes Day 10

Wang and Isola showed in 2020 that contrastive loss decomposes into two forces:

  • Alignment. The numerator pulls each query toward its positive.
  • Uniformity. The denominator pushes every query away from everything else, which spreads the embeddings over the sphere.

The uniformity term is the anisotropy fix, and it is not a side effect. Every negative in the denominator is a small instruction to occupy a different part of the space. Train long enough with enough negatives and the narrow cone opens up, cosine scores spread across a usable range, and the ordering starts carrying real information.

Which means the number you measured on Day 10 was not a bug. It was an untrained geometry, and you now know the exact mechanism that trains it.

The part that actually decides quality

Look again at the batch of in-batch negatives. They are random other passages. For the honey query, one of them is about TCP handshakes. Distinguishing honey from TCP is not a skill worth spending capacity on, and once the model can do it, those examples contribute almost nothing to the gradient.

The negatives that teach are the ones that look right and are not: a passage about nectar collection when the question is about dehydration. Everything in this lesson works, and it works far better or far worse depending entirely on where the negatives come from.

That is tomorrow, and it is the single biggest lever in the whole training pipeline: hard negatives.
exercise:
1. Feel the temperature. Write six lines: take the similarity list [0.80, 0.75, 0.70, 0.40, 0.10], divide by T, softmax it, and print the probability on the positive and the loss. Sweep T over 1.0, 0.2, 0.05, 0.01 and reproduce the table above. Then change the hardest negative from 0.75 to 0.79 and rerun. Notice which temperature still produces a gradient worth having.

2. Work out your own batch ceiling. For a 768-dimension model at sequence length 256, estimate the activation memory for one sequence, then work out how many fit in 80 GB. Compare that to the batch sizes papers report. The gap is the reason GradCache exists.

3. Look at real training data. Pull up a public retrieval dataset such as MS MARCO triples, or the training config of any sentence-transformers model on the Hub. Find the batch size, the temperature and where the negatives came from. Those three fields explain most of the quality difference between one embedding model and another.
